title: Suphan Buri-Ayutthaya 2-Day Trip: Old Towns & River Markets
metaDesc: A 2-day, 1-night road trip across Suphan Buri and Ayutthaya in Thailand. Day 1 hits the Sam Chuk and Kao Hong riverside markets; Day 2 covers Ayutthaya's old city, Wat Mahathat and Wat Chaiwatthanaram, with timings, distances and famous local eats.
keywords: Suphan Buri Ayutthaya trip, Sam Chuk Market, Ayutthaya old city, 2-day 1-night itinerary, riverside markets Thailand
h1:
Suphan Buri-Ayutthaya 2 Days 1 Night
Old Towns and River Markets
intro: Suphan Buri and Ayutthaya sit only about 60 km apart, roughly an hour's drive, so it's easy to fold them into a single trip. Spend the first day wandering the old markets along the Tha Chin River on the Suphan Buri side, then cross over on day two to the UNESCO World Heritage old city at Ayutthaya. Both are close to Bangkok and you can drive yourself, so there's no flight and no long road slog.

blocks.html: This trip is planned around driving yourself, because the sights in both provinces are spread out and public transport is a hassle to chain together. Leave Bangkok early, take Highway 340 straight into Suphan Buri first, knock out the old markets and the well-known temples on day one, then stay overnight in Suphan Buri town. On day two, loop back down toward Ayutthaya and cover the old city before heading home.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: Highway 340 between Ban Sali and Suphan Buri has road-widening construction in stretches right now, so always open a map and check traffic before you go. If you see a long band of red, you can bypass it via the Sali interchange instead, which stays clear.

blocks.text: Day one - Suphan Buri, old markets along the Tha Chin River

blocks.html: Suphan Buri is known for old riverside markets that people still actually live in, not newly staged tourist sets. On the first day we cover Sam Chuk Market in the late morning, stop by Wat Pa Lelai, then finish at Kao Hong Market in the afternoon.

items.note: It's roughly 100-110 km to Suphan Buri town, around 1.5-2 hours depending on traffic. Pull into a gas station for coffee along the way if you need it.

items.activity: Walk Sam Chuk Market, the hundred-year-old market in Sam Chuk district
items.note: An old wooden market on the Tha Chin River, open daily 08:00-17:00 with no entry fee. Weekdays are quiet and parking is easy; weekends are livelier but harder to find a spot.
Plenty to eat here, from noodles to braised five-spice duck to old-style sweets and traditional coffee. You can graze your way through the whole lane.

items.activity: Stop by the Khun Chamnong Chinarak House Museum in the market
items.note: An old wooden house turned living museum that tells the story of the Sam Chuk Chinese community of the past. Open during market hours.

items.activity: Drive into town to pay respects to Luang Pho To at Wat Pa Lelai Worawihan
items.note: A huge Buddha image in the Pa Lelai posture, around 23 meters tall. This temple is tied to the Khun Chang Khun Phaen literary epic and is open 08:00-17:00.

items.activity: Walk Kao Hong riverside market in Bang Pla Ma district
items.note: An old market with a feel similar to Sam Chuk but quieter, open around 08:00-17:00. There's an old watchtower you can climb for views over the Tha Chin River.

items.activity: Check in around Suphan Buri town and have dinner
items.note: The town has several hotels and riverside restaurants. Rest up for the Ayutthaya leg the next day.

blocks.text: Eats you shouldn't miss in Suphan Buri's old markets

blocks.html: Sam Chuk Market is heaven for anyone who loves to eat. We've ordered these by what locals and reviews mention most often, so you can just follow along instead of backtracking.

items.name: Duck noodles and braised five-spice duck in Sam Chuk Market
items.blurb: Braised five-spice duck and duck noodles are the market's signature dishes, with several long-running stalls lined up along the walkway. The broth is fragrant with five-spice and the duck is tender.

items.name: Traditional coffee and old-style sweets
items.blurb: A traditional coffee shop in an old wooden building, brewed fresh and eaten with pa thong ko (Chinese doughnut sticks) or Thai sweets. It's a classic scene at the hundred-year-old market that people stop to photograph.

items.name: Tha Chin River snakehead fish
items.blurb: Suphan Buri sits on the Tha Chin River, so fresh freshwater fish is on the menu. Riverside restaurants serve grilled snakehead and pla chon lui suan (snakehead with herbs and greens), a hearty meal worth trying at least once.

items.name: Suphan salee sponge cake
items.blurb: Salee, a light and fluffy sponge cake, is the province's signature take-home treat. You can buy it both in the markets and at souvenir shops in town, and it travels home easily.

items.name: Snacks in Kao Hong Market
items.blurb: Kao Hong Market has traditional Thai sweets, rice wrapped in lotus leaf, and snacks made by the local community. Prices are easy on the wallet and it's a good spot to graze in the afternoon.

blocks.text: Day two - Ayutthaya, the World Heritage old city

blocks.html: On the morning of day two, check out and drive down toward Ayutthaya. It's about 60 km from Suphan Buri town to the Ayutthaya city island, roughly an hour. Cover the key temples in the World Heritage historical park, then finish with some souvenirs before heading back.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Ayutthaya, the city island and riverside

items.activity: Check out, leave Suphan Buri, head for Ayutthaya
items.note: About 60 km, roughly 1 hour. You can stop for boat noodles as a late breakfast in Ayutthaya town.

items.activity: Wat Mahathat - the Buddha head in the bodhi tree roots
items.note: The highlight is the Buddha head cradled perfectly by the roots of a bodhi tree. It's inside the historical park, has an entry fee, and takes about an hour to walk around.

items.activity: Wat Phra Si Sanphet + Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit
items.note: The three chedis lined up in a row are the classic image of Ayutthaya, right next to Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit, which houses a large bronze Buddha. You can walk between them.
Ayutthaya is known for boat noodles. Well-known spots like Pa Lek Jao Kao and others in town serve a rich broth in small bowls, so you can order several.

items.activity: Wat Chaiwatthanaram on the Chao Phraya River
items.note: A Khmer-style riverside temple that looks its best in the evening light. Around the temple are shops renting Thai costumes for photos, and there's an entry fee.

items.activity: Buy roti sai mai to take home
items.note: Roti sai mai (cotton-candy roti) is Ayutthaya's signature souvenir. The famous shops are lined up in the row in front of the hospital, so pick the one you like and take some home.

items.activity: Walk Ayothaya Floating Market (if you've still got energy)
items.note: A floating market with a period feel, wooden Thai houses, food and souvenirs. It's a good way to wrap up before driving back to Bangkok, about 75 km away.

blocks.text: Make the most of Ayutthaya - know before you go

items: The temples on the city island are within walking distance — Wat Mahathat, Wat Ratchaburana and Wat Phra Si Sanphet are close together, so you can park once and walk between them.

Entry fees are charged per temple — the major temples in the historical park each charge separately, but a combined ticket is also sold. If you plan to hit several temples, the combined ticket works out cheaper.
Visit Wat Chaiwatthanaram in the evening — the light is nicer and there are fewer people than at midday. If you want to do a Thai-costume photo shoot, you can book a costume-rental shop ahead.
Dress respectfully — these are historical sites and sacred places, so skip spaghetti straps and overly short shorts.

blocks.title: You can trim it to a single day
blocks.html: If you only have one day, pick one or the other. Suphan Buri focuses on the old markets and Wat Pa Lelai, while Ayutthaya focuses on the temples on the city island. Cramming both provinces into one day feels too rushed to really soak up the atmosphere.

blocks.text: Extra stops if you have more time

blocks.html: If you stretch it to three days, or want to break up the drive, these two provinces have plenty more spots worth a stop. Pick whatever suits your style.

items.name: Bueng Chawak Chaloem Phrakiat
items.blurb: In Doem Bang Nang Buat district, with a freshwater and saltwater fish tunnel and a crocodile zone. Good for kids and takes about half a day.

items.name: Banharn-Jaemsai Tower
items.blurb: An observation tower in the middle of Suphan Buri town, over 120 meters tall. Take the lift up for views over the city in every direction.

items.name: Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon
items.blurb: A large chedi and a reclining Buddha in Ayutthaya. A popular stop to pray for blessings, just off the city island and not far away.

faq.q: How far apart are Suphan Buri and Ayutthaya, and is the drive long?
faq.a: From Suphan Buri town to the Ayutthaya city island is about 60 km, roughly a 1-hour drive. If you start from Bangkok and go to Suphan Buri first via Highway 340, that's about 1.5-2 hours, so it's easy to combine both provinces in one trip.

faq.q: How many days does this trip really need?
faq.a: Two days and one night is just right. Spend the first day on the old markets and temples in Suphan Buri and stay overnight in town, then cover Ayutthaya's old city on day two before heading back. If you only have one day, it's better to stick to a single province so you're not too rushed.

faq.q: What days is Sam Chuk Market open?
faq.a: Sam Chuk Market is open every day, 08:00-17:00, with no entry fee. Weekdays are quieter and parking is easier, while weekends are livelier with a fuller food spread but harder to park.

faq.q: What souvenirs are these two provinces known for?
faq.a: Suphan Buri's signature is fluffy salee sponge cake, while Ayutthaya is known for roti sai mai (cotton-candy roti) with many shops to choose from. Both are easy to take home and keep reasonably well.

faq.q: Do I need my own car for this trip?
faq.a: We'd recommend driving yourself or renting a car, because the sights in both provinces are spread out and public transport is hard to chain together, especially the old markets and temples outside the municipal area. Having a car makes it far more flexible.
